articles.title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
articles.summary: A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI to...
articles.body:
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.

It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut .

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.

"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.

He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.

"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."

Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.

The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.

"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."

Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.

In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.

"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."

Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.

Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

AP Technology Writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed.

articles.title: Quote of the day by businessman Marc Andreessen: "All of the technology required to transform industries through software finally works"
articles.summary: Decades of building layers of technical infrastructure and software services has been decades in the making – but is it about to unwind?
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

The turn of the millennium saw the world of business and technology change dramatically, with new levels of productivity unlocked due to the wider availability of software applications. This explosion of opportunity didn't happen overnight; it was many years in the making and when everything finally clicked, it fuelled a generational boom.

In his seminal essay in which he discussed the notion of software eating the world , Netscape co-founder Marc Andreessen also touched on all the breakthroughs that got us to where the world of software was at the time.

He highlighted that the software as a service (SaaS) boom would not have been possible without plenty of work behind the scenes, including the infrastructure of the internet and the rise of modern computing. Businesses, at the time, were only beneficiaries of the raft of accessible services because of the graft that had gone into laying the foundations.

During this time, traditional companies were being disrupted by software-driven competitors that adopted these technologies, with this approach a fixture for at least the next decade in the business world.

While this thesis remained intact for many years, it's fair to see things are crumbling under the weight of large language models in the latter half of the 2020s. Instead of humans using software to perform functions at work, these tasks can now be offloaded in a way that was never previously possible.

The years that have gone into building sophisticated software systems are also giving way to a rise of clones that people don't have to necessarily buy, but that they can build themselves by using an AI chatbot.

Similarly, the model of businesses commanding humans who leverage software is being replaced with a regime in which these functions are considered agentic resources that can be deployed.

articles.title: A birdwatcher in Canada spotted a rare songbird absent from his county for over five years; its leg bands revealed it hatched at a Smithsonian centre in Virginia and was released in Ontario
articles.summary: A routine drive along a county road in Ontario turned into an unexpected wildlife encounter for Canadian birdwatcher Paul Jones, who spotted a rather
articles.body: A routine drive along a county road in Ontario turned into an unexpected wildlife encounter for Canadian birdwatcher Paul Jones, who spotted a rather peculiar bird perched on an electrical wire in September. Initially thinking it might be a kingbird, Jones stopped his car and reached for his binoculars, hoping to get a closer look. What he found, however, was incredibly rarer. A loggerhead shrike (Lanius ludovicianus migrans), an endangered songbird in Ontario, had appeared in an area where the species had not been recorded for over five years.According to the Smithsonian's National Zoo, in a report dated November 10, 2026, Jones first noticed the bird's white wings, distinctive black facial mask and short, hooked bill. Recognising that it was not the bird he had initially suspected, he photographed it and recorded the coloured bands on its legs, which were orange over white on one leg and blue over metal on the other.A journey from Virginia to OntarioThe coloured bands proved to be an important clue in understanding where the bird had come from. Its history was already documented by the Smithsonian team, particularly animal keeper DJ Washington, who leads the institution's eastern loggerhead shrike breeding programme at its conservation campus in Front Royal, Virginia.The young bird had hatched on April 27, 2026, alongside 30 other chicks at the facility. A few months later, in mid-August, she was released at a field site operated by Wildlife Preservation Canada near Newburgh, Ontario. By the time Jones spotted her in September, the bird had travelled almost 30 miles south of the release location.This movement was an encouraging development, as the young shrike appeared to be beginning her autumn migration towards the United States.Washington described such public sightings as both amazing and validating, explaining that they offer confirmation that conservation work carried out within the facility can have an impact beyond its immediate surroundings.The little bird with an unusual hunting techniqueAt first glance, the loggerhead shrike might not look particularly intimidating. A small grey-and-white songbird, it is perhaps an unlikely candidate for the rather unusual nickname it has acquired: the butcherbird.The name comes from its distinctive way of catching and storing food. Unlike hawks and eagles, shrikes do not possess the powerful talons and sharp bills needed to tear apart their prey. Instead, they have developed an unusual hunting technique, impaling insects and small animals on sharp branches, thorns and even barbed wire fences.These makeshift food stores allow them to return to their prey later. The behaviour also has a role in territorial displays, with males sometimes using impaled prey to demonstrate their hunting abilities to potential mates and discourage competing birds from entering their territory. The Smithsonian's Washington has also ensured that birds raised in captivity have opportunities to practise these natural behaviours. Their surroundings include different perching options, including thorny branches and barbed wire, helping them develop the skills they will need after release.This subspecies, which extends from Canada into the southeastern United States, has witnessed a population decline of more than 70 per cent over the last 50 years.The conversion of grasslands and shrublands for intensive agriculture and urban development has affected the landscapes these birds depend on, both during breeding and while spending the winter. High mortality during migration and the widespread use of pesticides, which reduces the availability of their prey, have added to the pressures.To help reverse this decline, the Smithsonian joined Wildlife Preservation Canada's recovery programme in 2011. Since 2014, its staff have raised nearly 300 chicks, releasing more than 75 per cent of them into the wild. Wildlife Preservation Canada's biologist Helmi Hess estimates that conservation-bred birds have accounted for over 13 per cent of the wild shrike population over the past two decades. The organisation also reports that approximately 30 per cent of wild-hatched birds have at least one conservation-bred parent.When birdwatchers become part of conservationPerhaps one of the most encouraging aspects of this sighting is that it demonstrates how members of the public can contribute to wildlife research without necessarily being scientists themselves.Birdwatchers such as Jones help fill important gaps in the monitoring of migratory species, whose movements can be difficult to track. By photographing birds, recording their sightings and sharing observations through platforms such as eBird, they provide researchers with information that can help establish where particular species are appearing and how their populations are changing.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Superlua em Goiás: Veja o horário e como observar o fenômeno | G1
articles.standfirst: Primeira superlua de 2026 poderá ser observada a partir das 18h, segundo especialista. Lua poderá apresentar tons avermelhados e alaranjados, mas a presença de nuvens pode dificultar a visualização.
articles.summary: A superlua em Goiás poderá ser vista a partir das 18h desta terça-feira (24), apresentando cores vibrantes e um brilho intenso no horizonte leste do estado.
articles.body:
A primeira superlua de 2026 poderá ser observada no céu de Goiás nesta terça-feira (24). Segundo o Observatório Nacional (ON), a Lua Cheia ocorrerá às 11h53, no horário de Brasília, quando o satélite natural estará a 360.768 quilômetros da Terra. Apesar de a fase cheia acontecer durante o dia, o melhor momento para observar o fenômeno será no início da noite, a partir das 18h, segundo o astrofotógrafo Pedro Augusto.

Ao g1, Pedro explicou que a superlua acontece quando a Lua Cheia ocorre próxima ao perigeu, ponto da órbita em que o satélite natural fica mais perto da Terra. Nessa condição, ela pode parecer um pouco maior e mais brilhante do que o habitual.

Segundo o especialista, esta será a primeira superlua de 2026, e outra está prevista para dezembro. A Nasa também prevê uma sequência de três superluas, que continuará em janeiro de 2027.

Lua do Caçador é vista no céu do interior de Pernambuco — Foto: Marlon Tenório/Associação Astronômica de Arcoverde

O astrofotógrafo Pedro Augusto, que pretende fotografar a superlua em Goiânia nesta terça-feira (24), explica que o melhor horário para observar o fenômeno será a partir das 18h, quando a Lua começará a aparecer no horizonte. Não será necessário utilizar telescópios ou binóculos.

A recomendação é procurar locais abertos, com boa visibilidade para o horizonte leste, mesma direção em que o Sol nasce, e sem obstáculos, como prédios e árvores. O astrofotógrafo alerta, porém, que a presença de nuvens poderá dificultar tanto a observação quanto os registros do fenômeno.

"Quando a Lua está próxima ao horizonte, tem outros dois fenômenos que também maximizam a observação. O primeiro é que a Lua parece maior ainda, porque o nosso cérebro cria uma ilusão de ótica a partir da comparação do disco lunar com outras coisas que a gente vê na paisagem", explicou.

Pedro também destacou que a Lua poderá apresentar uma coloração diferente ao surgir no horizonte. Segundo ele, a passagem da luz pela atmosfera pode fazer com que o satélite apresente tons avermelhados ou alaranjados.

"São três coisas: a superlua, a ilusão de ótica e também a cor", resumiu.

Lua cheia com tons alaranjados próxima ao horizonte, em registro do astrofotógrafo Pedro Augusto. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Pedro Augusto

Por que a Lua de novembro é considerada uma superlua?

Embora seja conhecida popularmente como superlua, a classificação não possui uma definição astronômica oficial reconhecida pela União Astronômica Internacional (IAU).

Segundo a astrônoma Josina Oliveira do Nascimento, do Observatório Nacional, existem diferentes critérios para determinar quando uma Lua Cheia pode receber essa denominação.

A Lua desta terça-feira atende a apenas um dos três critérios apresentados pelo Observatório Nacional:

Distância da Terra: um dos critérios estabelece que a Lua precisa estar a até 360 mil quilômetros do planeta. No dia 24, estará a 360.768 quilômetros.

Intervalo até o perigeu: outro critério exige que a Lua Cheia aconteça até 12 horas antes ou depois do ponto de maior aproximação. Em novembro, a diferença será de aproximadamente 30 horas.

Proximidade orbital: o terceiro critério considera superlua quando o satélite está dentro da faixa de 10% das menores distâncias da Terra ao longo de sua órbita. A Lua de novembro atende a essa condição.

"O termo 'superlua' não é uma definição astronômica oficial, o que faz com que existam diferentes interpretações sobre qual lua cheia recebe essa denominação", explicou Josina.

A maior aproximação entre a Lua e a Terra ocorrerá na quarta-feira (25), às 18h02, cerca de 30 horas após o instante exato da Lua Cheia.

Por que a Lua parece maior e avermelhada?

Além da proximidade com a Terra, dois efeitos visuais podem chamar a atenção de quem observar a superlua logo após o nascimento no horizonte.

O primeiro é conhecido como ilusão lunar. Quando a Lua aparece próxima a elementos da paisagem, como árvores, prédios e montanhas, o cérebro humano pode interpretá-la como maior do que quando está no alto do céu.

O segundo efeito está relacionado à atmosfera terrestre. Quando a Lua está próxima ao horizonte, sua luz atravessa uma camada maior da atmosfera antes de chegar aos nossos olhos. Isso favorece a percepção de tons alaranjados e avermelhados.

A Nasa explica que esses efeitos também podem ser observados durante luas cheias comuns e não dependem exclusivamente da ocorrência de uma superlua.

A próxima superlua está prevista para 23 de dezembro, às 22h28, no horário de Brasília, segundo o Observatório Nacional.

Na ocasião, a Lua estará a aproximadamente 356.740 quilômetros da Terra, distância menor do que a registrada em novembro.

Diferentemente da superlua desta terça-feira, a de dezembro atenderá aos três critérios apresentados pelo Observatório Nacional, incluindo a distância inferior a 360 mil quilômetros e o intervalo de menos de 12 horas entre a fase cheia e o perigeu.

A Nasa também prevê outra superlua em janeiro de 2027, completando a sequência de três fenômenos consecutivos.

articles.title: Elon Musk's space ambitions are worrying SpaceX lenders, who do not want Tesla CEO to send their chips to ...
articles.summary: Elon Musk’s plans for orbital data centres are reportedly worrying SpaceX lenders.
articles.body: ​Elon Musk’s plans for orbital data centres are reportedly worrying SpaceX lenders. Investors backing the rocket company’s AI chip financing worth billions sought a clause to keep the Nvidia chips securing the debt on Earth, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Lenders feared that if SpaceX sent the chips into orbit and later defaulted, they would be unable to recover and sell the equipment to recoup their losses.​Musk has outlined plans to run AI models from satellites equipped with advanced chips. SpaceX says it plans to use the Nvidia equipment covered by the deal in data centres on Earth. However, the report could not verify whether the proposed restriction made it into the final financing documents.​The financing deal, known as “Project Saturn”, will fund Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems for SpaceX’s computing operations. Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, announced pricing for about $44 billion in notes and said strong investor demand had increased the deal size.​Elon Musk wants Starship to carry AI satellites into orbit​SpaceX’s plan for orbital data centres calls for a network of solar-powered satellites that would run AI workloads in orbit. At the Baron Investment Conference this month, Elon Musk said he expected a fully reusable Starship to bring down the cost of putting hardware into orbit. That matters because a data centre spread across satellites would require repeated launches to deploy the hardware and replace it as it ages.​In January, SpaceX applied to the US Federal Communications Commission for permission to launch and operate up to one million satellites for its orbital data centre system. The company’s ‘Starmind’ design calls for solar panels that face the Sun, radiators that shed heat into space and laser links that relay data through Starlink. Cooling is an engineering challenge because the vacuum offers no air to carry heat away from the chips.​Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s has already run an AI prompt in orbitGoogle CEO Sundar Pichai pointed to the appeal of near-continuous solar power in an October interview with Alex Heath. Some orbits let satellites spend nearly all their time in sunlight, giving them a steady power source for onboard computing. Google is testing the idea through Project Suncatcher, which uses its own AI chips, known as tensor processing units, or TPUs.​Google built its first prototype with satellite company Planet and launched it aboard a SpaceX rideshare mission last month. Later that month, Google said it sent a prompt to the satellite and received a haiku written onboard by its Gemma 4 model. The next test, planned for 2027, will use two interconnected satellites to see how they work together in orbit.This month, Google also announced that Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket would launch satellites each designed to provide roughly the computing capacity of a data centre rack. That launch is targeted for the first quarter of 2029.Fearless legend or grounded realist? Rate yourself on 11 categories in the Great Indian Confidence Survey – find out in 3–6 min

articles.title: COP31 has failed. The climate system is working as designed
articles.summary: The failure exposes a diplomacy that protects fossil-fuel power while leaving vulnerable countries to pay the price.
articles.body:
COP31 ended without an overarching agreement on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye, after nearly 200 countries failed to agree on a final climate pact. The proposed text could not even name the principal cause of global warming: fossil fuels. The European Union, several Pacific island states and other governments rejected it, while oil-producing countries resisted stronger language. After three decades of annual summits, this was the first such breakdown since 2009.

It is tempting to call this an extraordinary diplomatic failure. But the collapse reveals something more enduring. Climate negotiations have become remarkably effective at keeping governments at the table while avoiding the economic changes that meaningful climate action requires. The system is not designed literally to produce no agreements; it is designed to accommodate interests powerful enough to prevent decisive ones.

Consider what happened in Antalya. The EU objected that the final draft did not even mention fossil fuels. Yet the omission was not a clerical oversight. Earlier language on moving away from oil, gas and coal had been weakened as negotiations proceeded. The summit could not agree on how to implement the agreement reached at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. What should have been the starting point for action became the point at which diplomacy broke down.

The contradiction is built into the negotiating process. Under the Paris Agreement, governments determine their own emissions commitments, with no enforcement mechanism to compel a country to stop expanding fossil-fuel production. COP decisions also depend on consensus, giving determined holdouts considerable leverage. The result is an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do.

That does not mean all countries are equally responsible. Nor does it mean that every COP has achieved nothing. The Paris framework helped establish common goals, and climate summits have encouraged investment and cooperation. Antalya itself adopted limited decisions on other matters, including one on a just transition. But these gains cannot substitute for a credible timetable to wind down fossil-fuel extraction. The distinction matters: diplomatic activity is not the same as structural change.

Indeed, fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall. Producing states defend revenues and geopolitical influence, while consuming states continue to rely on cheap energy and established infrastructure. Even governments that speak forcefully about climate ambition face incentives to protect their own industries and voters from immediate costs. The global energy transition is therefore not simply a technological problem. It is a struggle over who must relinquish assets, profits and power.

This helps explain the appeal of technological promises. The failed Antalya draft promoted carbon-removal technologies to deal with warming beyond 1.5C, while disagreements also centred on carbon capture and storage. Such approaches may have limited roles in reducing or counterbalancing emissions from difficult-to-abate sectors. But when presented as substitutes for reducing extraction, they allow governments and corporations to promise that future machines will repair the damage of continued emissions. The political benefit is immediate; the promised atmospheric benefit remains uncertain.

The same structural inequality shapes climate finance. Countries that contributed least to historical warming face mounting costs from droughts, floods, displacement and adaptation. Yet the proposed $120bn adaptation target disappeared from the revised text and disputes over financial commitments helped sink the talks. Wealthy governments can celebrate climate ambition while leaving poorer countries to borrow, divert public spending or simply absorb losses.

This is precisely why climate finance cannot be treated as discretionary charity. It concerns responsibility for harms produced through an unequal world economy. Grants, predictable funding and meaningful decision-making power for affected countries are not extras to be negotiated after emissions targets. They are conditions of a transition that poorer countries can undertake without sacrificing education, healthcare and basic development.

There is also a danger in allowing the EU to emerge from Antalya as the uncomplicated defender of climate justice. Its refusal to accept a pact silent on fossil fuels was justified. But wealthy countries cannot demand ambitious language abroad while resisting the financial obligations and domestic changes that would give it substance. Conversely, some developing countries depend on fossil-fuel income or need affordable energy. A just phaseout must distinguish their circumstances from those of rich, historically high-emitting economies.

What would a different climate politics look like? It would begin with enforceable plans for ending new fossil-fuel expansion and phasing down production, with richer countries moving first and fastest. It would fund adaptation and loss and damage through reliable, primarily grant-based transfers rather than debt-creating loans. And it would give countries most vulnerable to climate change greater influence over the decisions that determine their futures.

None of this requires abandoning multilateralism. It requires refusing to confuse its survival with success. When consensus rules repeatedly protect the interests most responsible for the crisis, governments must also pursue complementary agreements, domestic regulation and coalitions willing to move faster. Otherwise, the promise of universal participation becomes a mechanism for universal delay.

The collapse of COP31 is a warning, not because climate diplomacy has suddenly stopped working, but because its limits have become impossible to disguise. The world does not lack knowledge of what causes warming. It lacks a political system willing to confront those who benefit from causing it. Until that changes, each summit will be judged by the agreements it produces, while the atmosphere registers the emissions it fails to prevent.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Anti-austerity strike spurs transport chaos across Belgium
articles.summary: National strike against planned austerity causes widespread disruption, with government’s fate hanging in the balance.
articles.body:
Transport services across Belgium have been disrupted, with hundreds of flights and trains cancelled , as trade unions called a national strike to protest against the federal government’s austerity measures.

Monday’s walkout grounded planes across the country after air traffic controller Skeyes said it was unable to provide regular services at Belgian airports.

In a statement on its website, Brussels airport said that “unfortunately, all departing and arriving flights from 7am to 9pm local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) will have to be cancelled”.

Air traffic was also halted on Monday at Brussels’ Charleroi airport, which is used by low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium, which represents about 25 carriers, said the strike would be the 11th affecting Belgian airspace in as many months.

The national strike has also caused disruption to buses, trains, schools, and other public services. Belgium has faced repeated cost-of-living protests and strikes in recent months, with much of the anger directed towards Prime Minister Bart De Wever and his attempts at cost-cutting.

The Belgian government is trying to save 10 billion euros ($10.9bn) in the coming years to reduce the country’s high deficit, but the issue is dividing the ruling coalition and threatens to collapse the government.

De Wever has already offered King Philippe his resignation, but the monarch refused to accept it, giving him more time to find a solution to the budget impasse. The prime minister has now set a new December 31 ⁠ ⁠⁠ ⁠deadline for his government to reach an agreement on next year’s budget, ⁠⁠⁠⁠after another week of talks ended without a result.

“Should we not have a budget agreement [before the end of the year], the ‌‌‌‌government will effectively be unable to govern, thereby bringing its existence to an end”, De Wever’s office said in a statement.

The government is looking at spending cuts, notably in healthcare, and a VAT increase to bring down the deficit, but unions have been pushing for taxes on high earners to offset some of the cuts, as protests against rising living costs continue, not only in Belgium but across Europe .

images.caption: Protesters take part in a demonstration as part of national strikes and protests movements against government austerity measures in Brussels, on November 23, 2026 [Nicolas Tucat/AFP]

articles.title: Meta throws out its net-zero goal — its competitors should be furious | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Meta walked back its 2030 net-zero goal in its 2026 sustainability report, a decision that could send ripples throughout the tech industry.
articles.body:
Meta’s new sustainability report buries the lead: The company is almost certain to miss its own goal to reach net zero by 2030, and it’s refusing to commit to a new timeline.

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets — so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net-zero and sustainability at Meta, in the introduction to the company’s 2026 sustainability report.

That’s a lot of words to say that Meta will continue to pollute if that means it can continue its AI rollout.

Such is the risk of voluntary targets. Companies can make and break them with little to lose, betting — often rightly — that they can ignore them with just a small hit to public opinion, which is fickle anyway. (Remember the Cambridge Analytica scandal? Most people don’t.) There’s almost no risk to the bottom line.

“We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline and interim milestone. We’ll continue investing in emissions reductions and reporting our progress annually,” a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch.

A few years ago, Meta was arguably one of the better corporate stewards of the climate. The company has been one of the largest purchasers of clean power, and it set ambitious goals for water conservation.

More recently, though, its multibillion-dollar bet on natural gas at its Hyperion data center in Louisiana has undone much of that progress. Natural gas may burn cleaner and more efficiently than coal, but its impact on global warming can be just as bad when the leaky infrastructure needed to burn it is factored in.

Despite years of clean power procurement, Meta’s greenhouse gas emissions have more than doubled in the last four years. Between 2024 and 2025, its data center emissions increased more than 12 times, and Hyperion isn’t online yet.

That commitment to natural gas led to the company’s departure from RE100 , a corporate renewable energy initiative, in July. The company had been part of the group for a decade, though the two split after RE100 started requiring more rigorous reporting toward renewable energy targets.

“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned,” they added. “The reality has been far more complex. Demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected, arriving on a timeline measured in quarters rather than decades, and meeting it has meant building at a pace and scale the industry has never attempted.”

That’s all true, but when put that way, it sounds like Meta has little agency in the matter. But the company’s decision to chase AI was a conscious one.

You could argue that Meta has a fiduciary duty to chase after its peers, which have also dived headfirst into AI. But there’s precious little data to support the idea that AI will be a profit driver for a company like Meta, which is almost entirely consumer-focused.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg is optimistic that improving Muse’s energy efficiency will turn that around, but how much will everyday people be willing to pay for software that translates your offhand thoughts into surreal memes? Or monitors your emails so you won’t forget to reply to your mom? Meta is betting that it’ll be enough to support a $200 billion-plus data center , and probably more.

The choice of the fuel to power those AI ambitions was also a conscious one. Natural gas power plants, besides being able to run 24/7, are actually not a great fit for AI data centers. Turbines like to run at constant speeds, while AI data centers’ energy requirements surge and sag depending on the load. They need batteries as a buffer, which begs the question: Why not just connect to the grid and use batteries to bridge any gaps during times of peak demand? That’s what one expert recommends .

Meta’s bet on natural gas appears mistimed. Long-duration energy storage is coming into its own — and geothermal energy appears poised to become the next major power source on the grid in the U.S. Companies like Fervo, Mazama, and Quaise have been logging milestones at a rapid clip , potentially unlocking tens of gigawatts of capacity. The technology isn’t competitive with natural gas today, but it very well could be in the mid-2030s, just a few years after Meta completes Hyperion. Geothermal is also not vulnerable to supply chain shocks, like what happened with natural gas and the Iran War.

Beyond that, the company’s decision to abandon its 2030 net-zero goal risks fomenting the sort of backlash that leads to regulations with real teeth. Such regulations won’t just apply to Meta, and the broader industry would be justified in their frustration.

In that light, Meta’s timing couldn’t be worse. Surveys show the general public doesn’t hold AI or data centers in high esteem, rightly sensing that the infrastructure development is driving a rapid and often-unchecked expansion of polluting infrastructure.

The tech industry has spent over a decade trying to prove that it would be different from previous industrial juggernauts like oil and gas or automobile manufacturing. In a single PDF, Meta might have undone much of that goodwill. After this, who will trust another tech company’s voluntary net-zero goals?

articles.title: The next space race is ours to win. Don’t blow it, Washington.
articles.summary: Florida Sen. Ashley Moody urged Congress to establish the new United States Space Academy in her state to leverage its existing aerospace infrastructure and expertise.
articles.body:
On Monday, Nov. 16, states across the country faced a deadline to express interest in becoming home to the new United States Space Academy.

America is in a new space race, and this time winning isn’t just about making history. Our military relies on satellites for communications, navigation, intelligence and early missile warning. Protecting those capabilities and maintaining America’s superiority in space are essential to our national defense.

The Space Academy will prepare the next generation of space leaders. Where they train and the expertise and infrastructure available to them will help determine how well equipped they are to meet the challenges ahead.

Where we establish this institution is a national security decision. Washington had better treat it like one. And when you consider what this academy needs to succeed, one state stands apart. The Space Academy belongs in Florida.

Florida isn’t asking Washington to gamble on what might be possible. We’re offering something better: generations of experience and a proven record of achievement.

From the first Mercury astronauts to this April’s Artemis II launch from Kennedy Space Center, Florida has been at the forefront of America’s journey into space, and we’re not slowing down.

In 2025, Florida’s Space Coast set a record with 109 orbital launches , more than any other spaceport in the country. Kennedy Space Center and Cape Canaveral Space Force Station operate side by side, supporting NASA, our military and America’s commercial space industry.

Nearby, Patrick Space Force Base is headquarters for the Space Force’s Space Training and Readiness Command, the command responsible for training and educating guardians.

Florida’s universities are building the next generation of aerospace talent. The University of Central Florida was founded to support America’s space program and partners with the Space Force. Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University and Florida Tech are developing the engineers, scientists and aerospace professionals our nation needs.

Together, these military, academic and commercial resources form a mature aerospace ecosystem built through decades of public and private investment.

The academy’s students should learn alongside the people designing, building, launching and operating the technologies that will shape America’s future in space.

You can build a campus anywhere. You cannot recreate this experience and these partnerships overnight.

And before Washington commits taxpayer dollars to building something new, somebody ought to ask a pretty basic question:

Why should American taxpayers pay to recreate launch ranges, test facilities and an industry base that already exist here?

The academy will require new investment. But every dollar wasted duplicating existing infrastructure is a dollar that could instead support instruction, research, advanced technology and the students themselves.

That’s why I introduced the STARS Act to establish the U.S. Space Academy in Florida.

Whereas some states have recently expressed reservations or outright hostility towards the future of space, Florida has offered a different record. We have maintained a consistent environment of clear rules, competitive costs, and practical support for both government and commercial space activity.

Investment in the next generation of space capability has repeatedly found solid ground here — not because of any single election cycle, but because the foundational conditions for success have stayed reliable.

That track record is why the new space academy belongs in the Sunshine State, where it has already been demonstrated that long-term investment in America’s future in space exploration will be treated as a priority rather than a political variable.

And I trust Republicans and Democrats alike can agree that this decision must be guided solely by national security, responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars and the academy’s long-term success. The academy should be no one’s political trophy. I’m ready to work with colleagues in both parties to make it happen.

President Trump understood what was at stake when he established the United States Space Force. The Space Academy is our opportunity to build on that legacy by preparing the next generation to defend America’s interests in space.

The infrastructure is here. The expertise is here. The manufacturers, researchers, military personnel and skilled workers who power America’s space program are here. We have spent generations building America’s gateway to space. Why on Earth would we start over somewhere else? The Space Academy belongs in Florida.

Ashley Moody is the junior U.S. senator from Florida.

images.caption: President Donald Trump holds up an order to create the U.S. Space Academy before a Congressional Space Medal of Honor ceremony at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Houston, as Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, right, look on. (AP Photo/Karen Warren)

articles.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
articles.summary: Oregon and Virginia are suing SpaceX, alleging that the company profited by failing to prevent its Grok AI model from generating nonconsensual sexual deepfakes.
articles.body: In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.” “Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.” The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors. xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however. Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages. The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors: > “The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”

articles.title: Court allows Army to go forward with planned detonation of toxic drums in Iowa
articles.summary: A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit.
articles.body: A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit. It is not clear when the detonation, which was most recently set for Wednesday, will happen. “We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide,” the order from the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals said. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.” The court said that the Environmental Protection Agency had adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead and that the Army had considered a full range of alternatives. “A controlled detonation with attendant safety measures better alleviates the risk of irreparable harm than the risk of an uncontrolled explosion,” the court said in lifting an administrative stay on the permit. The detonation, which would send a plume of lead dust across Iowa and likely into neighboring states, has raised fear and concern from residents who said they had not had enough time to prepare. Earlier Monday, President Donald Trump ordered the Army to pause its planned detonation until the court weighed in. “I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump said in a Truth Social post. The detonation was initially scheduled for Friday. After public outcry and a lawsuit from environmental groups last week, the Army delayed the detonation until Monday and then later pushed it again to Wednesday. The court last week gave an administrative stay in the case, putting the Army’s environmental permit to detonate on hold. But the Army told the court it could go forward with a detonation in an emergency without the court’s ruling. The Eighth Circuit ruling, released on Monday afternoon, will clear the way for the Army to go forward with the court’s blessing. The outcry over the federal government’s handling of the situation and the decision of whether to detonate had become something of a political football earlier on Monday afternoon. In his Truth Social post before the appeals court ruling, Trump seemed intent on deferring responsibility to Sand, who has not taken office yet. “If he or the Courts do not agree,” Trump said of Sand, “we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation.” Trump said military leaders had advised him that detonating the material soon was the safest option and that the weather forecast for Wednesday was optimal. “The Experts, who know it well, and have been studying it for many years, feel there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future,” Trump wrote. “The weather, right now, is optimal for this planned response to take place.” The Army has said it must detonate the 68 drums of deteriorating, toxic lead azide — a chemical used to make bomb triggers — at the Iowa ammunition plant because the chemical has undergone a process of “recrystallization” that has made it highly unstable and dangerous. The Army has said that it is unsafe to move the drums and that cold weather will further destabilize the material and could cause a spontaneous explosion. The Army had told Middletown residents that the blast could break windows and shake their homes. But residents elsewhere in Iowa — and in the plume’s potential path outside the state — said they didn’t learn about it until last week and were concerned for their families’ well-being, crops and pets. Lead is a potent neurotoxin for which there is no safe level of exposure. Airborne lead is an acute health risk, experts said, and once the metal gets deposited in soil or on surfaces, it can remain there forever unless it’s physically removed. Exposure to lead is associated with learning disabilities, reproductive problems, mental health issues and increased risk of hearing loss, among other effects. The long-term risks are particularly pronounced for young children. The Army said it had covered the bunker with two stories of sand in collapsible, modular barriers to dampen the effects of the explosion. Meanwhile, scientists, politicians and residents have been trying to figure out how the situation got so sideways and why the Army feels its only choice is a detonation, whether planned or unplanned. In a statement on X before the court’s ruling, Sand said the administration should make its decision “based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago” and who have been in Middletown for weeks. Sand implied that the administration might have information about the urgency of the situation that is not known publicly. “Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” Sand said. “That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I’ve asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible.” An Army spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Iowa residents said they were growing frustrated with the twists and turns of the detonation saga. Debra Ott, who works at Fat Annie’s August Tap, which is about a quarter-mile from a gate that leads into the ammunition plant, said she was planning to stay inside for a full day if and when the detonation takes place. “I have some heart issues, and I have a hard enough time breathing anyway. So whenever they do it, I plan on staying in the house 24 hours because I don’t want to be out,” Ott said. “The bean dust and corn dust around here is bad enough without lead.” Ott, who lives in Augusta, Iowa, about 5 miles from Middletown, said she was growing tired of the scheduling changes for detonation and increasingly concerned about a spontaneous explosion. “I don’t want to be sitting at home at midnight and have it go off and not have a clue what’s going on without anybody up there to try to control it. If they’re going to do it, I wish they just do it and quit changing it every day,” she said. Ott lives with her granddaughter and her granddaughter’s three young children, who are 13, 4 and 2. “We’ll hose down all the outside stuff and wipe off, you know, wipe down the doorknobs and anything the vehicles, anything the kids can touch with their hands, where they could get it in their mouth,” Ott said. “We just don’t know what to expect because we don’t know when they’re going to do it.” The trajectory of the dust plume depends on the direction and strength of the wind, so each delay puts a new group of people in the path of the expected hazard. “It’s just very frustrating,” said Jill Holler, who lives about 50 miles from Middletown, in Muscatine, Iowa, which could be in the path of the lead dust plume, depending on the wind. Holler, whose family has a farm about 20 miles west of Middletown where they raise cattle and grow soybeans and corn, said she was racing to gather soil samples ahead of the blast Sunday night. Understanding the lead content present in soil before the blast could help determine if a property is affected and what remediation might be needed. “We thought it would be tomorrow. So I was down in the dark getting the soil samples and it just, it’s frustrating,” Holler said on Monday. “It’s just strange, and you just never know what the next day is going to bring, and so you never. You’re, you’re pretty confident there’s going to be something else changing, and we can’t really believe what the next thing they say is going to happen.” Holler said she was most sympathetic to the people of Middletown, who are essentially living with a threat in their backyards that the Army has indicated could spontaneously explode. “If there really is an imminent threat and it’s very dangerous to explode at any time,” Holler said. “But it seems like they’re delaying, so it just isn’t adding up. It doesn’t make sense. So I think there’s going to have to be some explanation of what’s been going on.”

articles.title: An unidentified object excavated from a British cave in the 19th century has finally been identified as a 15,000-year-old seal-tooth pendant; researchers say it offers clues to ancient human culture and long-distance connections
articles.summary: An unidentified object recovered from a British cave during a 19th-century archaeological excavation has finally been recognised as a prehistoric piece of
articles.body: An unidentified object recovered from a British cave during a 19th-century archaeological excavation has finally been recognised as a prehistoric piece of jewellery. Researchers have identified the artefact as a pendant made from the tooth of a grey seal, dating back approximately 15,000 years. The discovery, made at Kents Cavern in Devon, is offering fresh insights into how people living towards the end of the last Ice Age created personal ornaments, travelled across long distances and maintained connections with communities beyond their immediate surroundings.15,000-year-old seal-tooth pendant remained unidentified for more than a centuryThe unusual artefact was originally discovered in 1867 during excavations at Kents Cavern in Torquay, Devon. The archaeological work was led by William Pengelly, whose investigations between 1865 and 1880 helped establish more systematic methods of recording archaeological discoveries in Britain.Despite being recovered alongside other prehistoric finds, the small tooth-shaped object did not attract much attention. It was initially believed to have come from an animal such as a badger, wolf or beaver. Its actual identity remained uncertain for more than 150 years.According to the Natural History Museum, renewed examination of the museum's archaeological collections eventually brought the overlooked object back into focus. Researchers from the Natural History Museum and University College London (UCL) revisited the artefact using modern scientific techniques to understand its origin and purpose.Their investigation established that it was made from the tooth of a grey seal, scientifically known as Halichoerus grypus. The research, published in the journal Quaternary Science Reviews, places the pendant at approximately 15,000 years old.The discovery is particularly important because objects made from seal teeth are extremely uncommon in prehistoric Britain.What did researchers discover about the pendant's manufactureResearchers also examined how the tooth had been modified and whether it had actually been worn by someone.As explained by UCL, the team used non-destructive techniques, including high-powered microscopy, 3D-modelling and micro-CT scanning. These methods allowed them to study the object's surface, internal structure and manufacturing marks without damaging the fragile artefact.The examination revealed that the tooth had been deliberately shaped. Much of its root had been scraped or ground away, making it thinner and smoother than its original form.A small hole had also been drilled through the remaining root. According to the Natural History Museum, the markings suggest that a pointed flint tool was repeatedly turned against the tooth while it was held in place. This would have required considerable care because the root could easily have split during the process. The hole provided space for a cord to pass through, allowing the tooth to hang from a necklace or bracelet.Researchers also cited evidence of long-term use. The surface had been rubbed smooth, polished, and the originally circular hole had slowly changed to an oval shape from the friction of a cord inside. These details indicate that the pendant was worn for a long time.Why does the inland discovery matter for understanding ancient connectionsOne of the most interesting aspects of the discovery is the location where the pendant was found.Kents Cavern is situated well inland, and the coastline was much farther away when the ornament was made. According to UCL, the ancient shoreline was up to 125 kilometres from the cave around that period. This raises questions about how an object made from a marine animal reached a location so far from the sea.Researchers have suggested two possible explanations. The pendant owner may have traveled a long way, perhaps following migrating animals or between different areas. The ornament could also have been exchanged between communities.The Natural History Museum says ancient people were not always confined to the immediate vicinity of their settlements. The movement of animal remains, ornaments and other materials indicates that communities were able to keep up links over great distances. The pendant provides evidence of how objects and cultural practices may have travelled between groups during the Upper Palaeolithic period.Similar discoveries reveal wider cultural links across EuropeThe Devon discovery also fits into a broader pattern of prehistoric ornament-making across Europe.According to the Natural History Museum, the period between approximately 21,000 and 13,000 years ago saw an increase in the use of bones and teeth from marine mammals to produce decorative objects.Archaeological discoveries at Las Caldas in Spain, for example, include several artefacts made from seals and whales. The site is located more than 40 kilometres inland, suggesting that marine animal materials were transported away from coastal areas.Researchers have also identified representations of marine mammals at Gönnersdorf in Germany, where seals were engraved into rocks hundreds of kilometres from the sea. Another nearby site, Andernach, contains a similar engraving alongside a whale-bone artefact.UCL notes that the newly identified Devon pendant is the first confirmed example of a Magdalenian-style seal-tooth pendant in the British Isles. Similar objects have been identified at archaeological sites in France and Spain.The Natural History Museum's human evolution expert Dr Silvia Bello, who co-authored the research, has suggested that the pendant may have had a social or symbolic role. It could have represented the identity of its owner or indicated an association with a community familiar with coastal environments.Only 4 other seal-tooth pendants from this period are currently known, making the Devon example particularly unusual.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks
articles.summary: Global negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to get a grip on AI’s energy demand at what advocates called the “worst” UN climate summit yet.
articles.body: The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday. Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric. To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy. “Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit. Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice). With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever. To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside. Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency. “That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event. In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found. To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation. Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall. “In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?” There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. The list of countries that includes, however, hasn’t been published yet, Carbon Brief reports. Another voluntary pledge to keep AI from derailing climate action by calling on data centers to run on less polluting energy also failed to garner much support. Douglas notes that by using the term “low-emission energy,” the pledge still leaves the door open for natural gas (which produces less carbon pollution than coal when burned but is a significant source of methane pollution) to keep powering data centers. “The Antalya A.I. pledge is a step in the right direction to address an important piece of the impacts, but needs teeth in order to translate into stronger protections for people and the planet,” the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council said in a statement when the pledge was first announced. “The speed, scale and scope of this challenge is bigger than perhaps anything before it, and the guardrails must be commensurate.”
